concepts.name: Mauryan Court Art vs. Popular Art: Classification and Distinction
key_dimensions: Defining characteristics of court art (royal patronage, polished stone, monumental scale) vs. popular/folk art (terracotta, unpolished, local themes)
Examples of each category and their geographic distribution
UPSC trap: Yaksha/Yakshi figures straddling both categories depending on context
Significance of this distinction in understanding Mauryan cultural plurality

concepts.name: Mauryan Pillars: Structural Composition and Symbolism
key_dimensions: Structural anatomy: monolithic shaft, bell-shaped (inverted lotus) capital, abacus, and crowning animal
Symbolism of each component — lotus as purity, animals as Dhamma symbols, abacus friezes
Material: use of Chunar sandstone and its significance for the polished finish
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Mauryan pillars (monolithic, polished) from later pillars like Gupta-era pillars

concepts.name: Sarnath Lion Capital: Iconographic and National Symbol Analysis
key_dimensions: Original composition: four lions, abacus with four animals (horse, bull, elephant, lion) and Dharma Chakras, and the inverted lotus base
Adopted as National Emblem of India — what was retained and what was altered (inverted lotus dropped)
The Dharma Chakra on the abacus vs. the Dharma Chakra on the National Flag — distinction in context
UPSC trap: The National Emblem motto 'Satyameva Jayate' is from Mundaka Upanishad, not inscribed on the original capital

concepts.name: Mauryan Polished Stone Technique ('Mauryan Polish')
key_dimensions: Technical description: mirror-like finish achieved through a distinct polishing technique, possibly using a mixture of materials
Materials predominantly used: Chunar sandstone for pillars, grey sandstone for sculptures
Geographical and chronological exclusivity — this technique virtually disappears after the Mauryan period
UPSC trap: Mauryan polish appears on both pillars AND free-standing sculptures (Didarganj Yakshi), not just pillars

concepts.name: Didarganj Yakshi: Style, Significance, and Attribution Debates
key_dimensions: Physical description: chauri-bearer, voluptuous form, transparent drapery, Mauryan polish — hallmarks of court art
Attribution controversy: some scholars date it to the Mauryan period, others to the Shunga or Kushan period based on stylistic analysis
Current location: Patna Museum — significance for questions about museum collections
Comparison with Parkham Yaksha to understand the range of Mauryan sculptural vocabulary

concepts.name: Parkham Yaksha and the Tradition of Yaksha-Yakshi Worship
key_dimensions: Description: massive, colossal form, frontal (en face) posture, cubic and block-like — contrast with the fluidity of Didarganj Yakshi
Yaksha-Yakshi cult as a pre-existing folk tradition that Mauryan art absorbed and monumentalized
Inscriptions on Parkham Yaksha identifying it as a community-commissioned work (not royal patronage) — significance for popular art tradition
UPSC trap: Parkham Yaksha lacks Mauryan polish, placing it in the popular art tradition despite its scale

concepts.name: Ashokan Edicts and Pillars: Relationship Between Text and Sculpture
key_dimensions: Not all Ashokan pillars bear edicts, and not all edicts are on pillars (some on rocks) — critical distinction
Pillars as vehicles of Dhamma propagation: the sculptural program (animal capitals) reinforces the textual message
Geographic distribution of pillar edicts vs. rock edicts and what it reveals about Mauryan administrative reach
UPSC trap: The pillar at Vaishali has no edict inscription but is a significant Mauryan sculptural monument

concepts.name: Animal Capitals on Mauryan Pillars: Symbolism and Regional Variations
key_dimensions: Known animal capitals: Lion (Sarnath, Sanchi, Rampurva), Bull (Rampurva), Elephant (Sankissa), Horse (debated/lost)
Symbolic meaning of each animal — lion as Buddha/royalty, elephant as Maya's dream/birth of Buddha, bull as the sign under which Buddha was born
UPSC trap: Not all pillars have the same animal — Rampurva has TWO pillars (one with bull capital, one with lion capital)
The Vaishali pillar with a single lion facing north — direction symbolism toward Lumbini (Buddha's birthplace)

concepts.name: Mauryan Terracotta Tradition: Characteristics and Contrast with Court Art
key_dimensions: Terracotta figurines as representatives of 'popular' Mauryan art — hand-modeled, mold-made, depicting mother goddesses, animals, and folk figures
Geographic spread: found across the Gangetic plain, indicating a pan-regional folk tradition
Contrast with court art: no royal patronage, no Mauryan polish, local materials, organic forms
Continuity: terracotta tradition predates and outlasts the Mauryan empire, showing cultural persistence beyond political changes

concepts.name: Lomas Rishi Cave and Rock-Cut Architecture as Sculptural Expression
key_dimensions: Lomas Rishi as the earliest surviving example of rock-cut architecture in India (Barabar Hills, Bihar)
Sculptural details: the entrance facade with elephant frieze and chaitya arch motif — considered the earliest representation of the chaitya arch in Indian art
Constructed for the Ajivikas (not Buddhists) — UPSC trap on religious patronage
The horseshoe-arch doorway as a precursor to later Buddhist chaitya hall facades, showing formal influence

concepts.name: Foreign Influences on Mauryan Sculpture: Achaemenid and Hellenistic Connections
key_dimensions: Similarities with Achaemenid Persian art: bell-shaped capitals, addorsed animal capitals, polished stone technique, monumental pillars
Possible influence route: Chandragupta Maurya's contact with Seleucid empire; diplomatic missions
Hellenistic influence: the realistic modeling of animals (especially the lion at Sarnath) showing naturalistic Greek-influenced rendering

UPSC trap: Despite foreign influences, Mauryan art has distinctive Indian elements — the abacus motifs (geese, honeysuckle) are Indian interpretations, and the overall program is Buddhist/Indian in intent

concepts.name: The Sarnath Lion Capital's Abacus: Iconographic Details
key_dimensions: Four animals on the abacus in the four cardinal directions: lion (south), horse (west), bull (east), elephant (north) — each separated by a Dharma Chakra
Each animal may represent a different Buddhist symbol or the four directions of Dhamma's spread
The 24-spoked Dharma Chakra on the abacus — this is distinct from the 24-spoked wheel on the Indian flag (inspired by it)
UPSC trap: The number of spokes — Sarnath abacus chakras have 24 spokes; the Indian flag's Ashoka Chakra also has 24 spokes, a direct adoption

concepts.name: Chunar Sandstone Quarries: Material Significance in Mauryan Art
key_dimensions: Location: Chunar, near Varanasi (modern Uttar Pradesh) — the primary source of fine-grained sandstone for Mauryan pillars
Properties enabling Mauryan polish: fine grain, homogeneous texture, amenability to polishing
Evidence of centralized state control: transportation of monolithic shafts over hundreds of kilometers implies state logistics
UPSC trap: Not ALL Mauryan sculptures use Chunar sandstone — some use local grey sandstone (e.g., Didarganj Yakshi possibly uses Chunar, but other figures use different stone)

concepts.name: Bodh Gaya Railings and Early Aniconic Buddhist Symbolism in Mauryan Sculpture
key_dimensions: Early Buddhist art (including Mauryan period) is ANICONIC — Buddha is represented through symbols (footprints, Bodhi tree, wheel, empty throne, umbrella)
The Bodh Gaya stone railing fragments attributed to the Mauryan period represent the earliest stone railings in Buddhist art
UPSC trap: Figural representation of Buddha does not begin until the Kushana period (Mathura and Gandhara schools) — Mauryan and Shunga art is aniconic
This aniconic tradition reflects a philosophical/doctrinal stance, not a lack of artistic capability

concepts.name: Sanchi Stupa and its Mauryan Core: Attribution and Later Additions
key_dimensions: The original Sanchi Stupa (Stupa No. 1) was built by Ashoka — a simple hemispherical brick structure
Later enlargement (Shunga period) and the addition of stone railings (vedika) and gateways (toranas) came AFTER the Mauryan period
UPSC trap: The famous sculptural toranas at Sanchi are Shunga/Satavahana-era, NOT Mauryan — only the brick core is Mauryan
Significance: Sanchi as a palimpsest of Indian art history, with Mauryan foundations underlying later artistic elaboration

concepts.name: Pataliputra Capital: Evidence of Hellenistic-Mauryan Artistic Synthesis
key_dimensions: The Pataliputra capital (found at Patna/Pataliputra, now in Patna Museum): a bracket-shaped capital with palmette (honeysuckle) and scroll motifs — strongly Hellenistic/Achaemenid in decorative vocabulary
Unlike the pillar capitals, this was not a crowning element of a free-standing pillar — its function is debated (possibly part of a palace structure)
It demonstrates that Hellenistic decorative motifs were incorporated into palace/court architecture, not just commemorative pillars
UPSC trap: The Pataliputra capital is distinct from the pillar capitals — it represents palace art, while pillar capitals represent commemorative/religious art

concepts.name: Mauryan Palace Architecture at Pataliputra: Sculptural and Artistic Context
key_dimensions: Megasthenes' account of Pataliputra palace and its comparison with Achaemenid Persepolis/Susa — literary evidence for understanding sculptural context
Archaeological finds: wooden palisade remains, stone column fragments suggesting a hypostyle hall
The polished stone columns of the Pataliputra palace as extensions of the same Mauryan court art tradition seen in Ashokan pillars
UPSC trap: Most of the palace is unexcavated or lost — much of our knowledge is from literary sources (Megasthenes, Arthashastra), not archaeology

concepts.name: Rampurva Bull Capital: Stylistic Naturalism and Comparison with Sarnath Lions
key_dimensions: The Rampurva bull capital: considered the finest example of animal sculpture in Mauryan art for its naturalistic rendering, muscular vitality, and three-dimensionality
Comparison with Sarnath lion capital: Sarnath lions are more stylized/heraldic; Rampurva bull is more naturalistic — raises question of different workshops or chronology
Current location: the bull capital is in the Rashtrapati Bhavan museum complex
UPSC trap: Rampurva site had TWO pillars — one with a bull capital and one with a lion capital; the lion capital from Rampurva is in the Indian Museum, Kolkata

concepts.name: Mauryan Sculpture and the Spread of Buddhism: Art as State Policy
key_dimensions: Ashoka's use of monumental sculpture (pillars, stupas) as instruments of Dhamma propagation — art serving a political-religious agenda
Geographic placement of pillars along trade routes and pilgrimage circuits — deliberate state planning
The sculptural program (Dharma Chakra, Buddhist symbols, edicts) as a unified communication strategy — India's earliest example of state-sponsored public communication
UPSC trap: Ashokan art serves Buddhism but also reinforces imperial authority — the lion (symbol of royalty) on the capitals conflates Dhamma and kingship

concepts.name: Post-Mauryan Continuity and Decline of Mauryan Sculptural Traditions
key_dimensions: The Mauryan polish technique disappears almost entirely after the Mauryan period — no satisfactory explanation has been established
Stylistic continuity: the colossal yaksha-yakshi tradition, the aniconic Buddhist symbols, and the railing motifs continue into Shunga and Satavahana art
The shift from court-patronized monumental stone sculpture to community-patronized sculpture in Shunga period — political and economic explanation
UPSC trap: The Shunga period is often seen as a 'decline' but is more accurately a democratization/decentralization of artistic patronage, not a decline in quality
